title: A Witness for the Portrait
premise: Ulyana Underhill, the meticulous archivist of St. Verena's Cathedral, is asked to authenticate the diary of Edith Marlowe, a verger who vanished eleven years ago into the cathedral's sealed crypt — a case the diocese declared closed when her body was never found. But the diary's final entries are written in a hand that continues for months after Edith's disappearance, and Ulyana realizes someone else has been living under her name. As they trace the forger through the cathedral's records, they uncover that Edith never vanished at all: she staged her death to escape a powerful canon, and the 'forger' is Edith herself, still hiding in plain sight among the congregation. In the crypt's locked dark, Ulyana must choose between exposing the truth and protecting the woman whose loyalty to the cathedral mirrors their own — closing the case by finally telling it honestly.
about_author: B. M. Yarrow spent a decade cataloguing parish archives in northern England before turning to fiction, a career that left them with an archivist's patience and a novelist's suspicion of tidy records. They write mysteries about people who mistake silence for safety.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Small Certainties
chapters.summary: POV Ulyana. The diocese delivers Edith Marlowe's recovered diary for authentication ahead of a memorial service, and Ulyana, proud of their flawless record of closed cases, begins cataloguing its contents. The emotional beat is quiet confidence — the pleasure of an ordered world — undercut by one small wrongness: the ink changes color on the last page.

chapters.title: Ink That Outlived Its Owner
chapters.summary: POV Ulyana. Forensic comparison shows the final entries were written over two years after Edith disappeared — same handwriting, different hand pressure. Ulyana interviews the retired dean who closed the case and catches him lying about the crypt seal. The beat shifts from confidence to unease: the archive itself is testifying against its keepers.

chapters.title: What the Crypt Keeps
chapters.summary: POV Ulyana. Breaking protocol, Ulyana enters the sealed crypt and finds it empty except for a hidden cache: Edith's real belongings, including a photograph of the canon who once ran the cathedral. Someone has been maintaining this space. The beat is dread mixed with exhilaration — the first proof the official story was built on nothing.

chapters.title: A Face Among the Congregation
chapters.summary: POV alternating Ulyana and 'Mrs. Pell,' a quiet elderly volunteer. Ulyana notices Mrs. Pell's intimate knowledge of spaces she shouldn't know; Mrs. Pell's chapters reveal a woman rehearsing a dead woman's memories each morning to keep them sharp. The beat is dramatic irony tightening like a wire.

chapters.title: The Canon's Confession, Undelivered
chapters.summary: POV Ulyana. Digging into diocesan correspondence, Ulyana finds Canon Ambrose Vell's letters implying he drove Edith out after discovering something about her — and that his own deathbed confession was suppressed by the current dean. Loyalty to the institution begins to curdle. The beat is betrayal.

chapters.title: Two Women, One Name
chapters.summary: POV Mrs. Pell. We learn the truth: Mrs. Pell IS Edith, living under an assumed identity, writing the diary's later entries as a private act of witness because no one else would remember her truthfully. She knows Ulyana is close. The beat is fear braided with defiance — memory as the last territory she owns.

chapters.title: Deadline at the Memorial
chapters.summary: POV Ulyana. The dean announces the memorial will include sealing the crypt permanently behind new stonework, destroying everything inside. Ulyana has days to decide whether to publish findings that will ruin the cathedral they love. The beat is the loyalty-versus-truth theme made explicit and urgent.

chapters.title: The Handshake in the Dark
chapters.summary: POV both. On the crypt's final night, Ulyana confronts Edith; instead of exposure, they strike a bargain: Ulyana will authenticate the whole diary as genuine — all of it, every year — if Edith consents to be named as alive. Both must surrender something: identity for one, certainty for the other.

chapters.title: Stone Over Stone
chapters.summary: POV Ulyana. At the sealing ceremony, the dean discovers the cache removed and accuses Ulyana of theft before the congregation. Ulyana publicly reads the diary's true final entry aloud, forcing the diocese to acknowledge Edith's survival rather than prosecute. The beat is climax: truth spoken in the one room that couldn't contain it.

chapters.title: A Witness for the Portrait
chapters.summary: POV Ulyana, coda weeks later. The case is reclosed — correctly this time — with Edith's consent and the dean's quiet resignation. Ulyana files the authenticated diary in the open archive, unsealed, and visits Edith, now simply herself. The beat is resolution: identity restored not by records, but by being witnessed.
